Enum Class PrecisionLossPolicy

java.lang.Object
java.lang.Enum<PrecisionLossPolicy>
dev.hardwood.writer.PrecisionLossPolicy
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, Comparable<PrecisionLossPolicy>, Constable
@Experimental public enum PrecisionLossPolicy extends Enum<PrecisionLossPolicy>

What RowWriter does with a value carrying more precision than the column it is written to can hold — an Instant with microseconds into a TIMESTAMP(MILLIS) column, a BigDecimal with three decimals into a DECIMAL(_, 2) column.

This governs precision only. A value the column cannot represent at all — a date beyond the INT32 day range, an unscaled decimal wider than the declared precision, an INT(8) out of range, a FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY of the wrong length — is rejected under every policy, because there is no truncation that would preserve its magnitude.

The policy applies to the row-oriented layer, which converts logical-type values to their physical representation. The columnar ColumnBatch API takes physical values and converts nothing, so nothing there can lose precision.

This API is Experimental: the shape may change in future releases.

  • Enum Constant Details

    • REJECT

      public static final PrecisionLossPolicy REJECT

      Reject the value, naming the field and the column's declared unit or scale. The default: a narrowing that loses digits is more often a mistake about the schema than an intention, and the two ways to state the intention — narrowing the value at the call site (instant.truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.MILLIS), decimal.setScale(2, …)) or selecting this policy — both leave a trace a reader of the code can see.

      A value that happens to be exact at the column's unit or scale is written normally; only one that would actually lose digits is rejected.

    • TRUNCATE

      public static final PrecisionLossPolicy TRUNCATE

      Drop the digits the column cannot hold, and write the value.

      • TIME and TIMESTAMP: the sub-unit fraction is dropped. The fraction is never negative — the value is carried as a whole-second count plus a nanosecond-of-second — so the written instant is the original floored to the column's unit. This is what Instant.toEpochMilli() does with the same value.
      • DECIMAL: the value is rescaled with RoundingMode.DOWN, dropping the digits beyond the declared scale rather than rounding to the nearest, so the written value is never larger in magnitude than the one handed over.

      Neither conversion rounds to the nearest representable value: both drop the digits that do not fit. The two differ on where a negative value lands — a timestamp floors toward the past, matching every other Parquet writer, while a decimal truncates toward zero, which is what dropping its trailing digits means.
